title: Discovery: Reliability & incident tolerance - Elysium Ventures
summary: Intro discovery on reliability and incident tolerance. Elysium runs low-latency customer-facing inference; primary concerns: multi-region failover, automated fallbacks to cheaper/compatible model variants, consistent latency under partial outages, and SLA expectations for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Redwood AE/SE explained routing policies, prefix/KV caching, model variants and canary rollouts, dedicated capacity SLAs, and private deployment networking/keys. Agreed next steps: share SOC2/security pack, schedule a 1-day benchmark (Daniel to run), and follow-up pricing for a 3-month Dedicated pilot.
topics: SLA expectations for Hosted vs Dedicated
next_steps: Daniel Kim to run 1-day throughput/latency benchmark with Elysium sample dataset and share results - target 2026-11-16
Maya to share SOC2, ISO attestation, and security whitepaper - target 2026-11-12
Schedule Dedicated pilot pricing call and contract outline - target 2026-11-18
action_items: Daniel Kim - run 10k token/day benchmark + failover scenario test - 2026-11-16
Maya Patel - send SOC2 report, network diagrams, and pilot pricing - 2026-11-12
Sanjay Rao - provide sample prompt set and success criteria for latency/quality - 2026-11-13
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-11-09 | Start: 15:30 PST | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (CTO, Elysium), Lena Ortiz (Head of Platform), Mike Chen (SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey thanks everyone for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I run the accounts for our mid-market segment. Today with me is Daniel, our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:16] Sanjay Rao: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited — want to focus on reliability and fallback strategies, run through how Redwood handles incidents.
[00:26] Daniel Kim: Awesome. Quick agenda: multi-region routing, fallbacks to model variants, caching behaviors, and SLA differences between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. We'll keep it casual — interrupt anytime.
[00:38] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. For context: Elysium serves customer-facing recommendation and conversational features, sub-200ms p50 is ideal, p95 under 400ms. We do have spikes and occasional region blips.
[00:50] Mike Chen: And we need to know what automatic failover looks like, how state (like KV cache) behaves across regions.
[01:03] Maya Patel: Totally. So high-level: Redwood has smart routing with region awareness and policy layers — you can route by latency, cost, or tier. In Hosted we have multi-region endpoints; in Dedicated you get reserved pools that can be multi-AZ or multi-region depending on config; Private is fully customer-managed but we ship control-plane integrations.
[01:25] Sanjay Rao: When you say "smart routing" — if a region goes fully down, do requests automatically go to another region? What's the RTO?
[01:36] Daniel Kim: Yes, automatic failover is supported. We track health checks and have per-route fallbacks. RTO is typically a few seconds to re-route, though TCP reconnections and warm caches impact cold latency. We recommend a small cross-region buffer — like 5–10% traffic to the secondary region during canary windows to keep warm caches.
[01:55] Lena Ortiz: Is that something Redwood configures or do we manage it?
[01:59] Maya Patel: We provide routing policies you can manage via the Console or API. For pilots we can set sane defaults. For Dedicated, we can also configure sticky routing and reserve burst capacity in a second region.
[02:14] Mike Chen: On the cache point — if KV cache is local to the GPU serving instance, do you replicate the KV across regions or is it prefix-cache-only per region?
[02:27] Daniel Kim: Currently KV is local to a serving pool. We have prefix/KV caching that reduces token work for repeated prompts; cross-region replication is not automatic because of latency tradeoffs. Instead we suggest warm-up routing and progressive traffic shifting. For stateful session continuity we support passing cached keys back to clients or externalizing the cache via a customer-managed store in Private deployments.
[02:55] Sanjay Rao: Hmm, externalizing cache adds complexity. If a primary region fails, will the secondary region start cold and spike latency?
[03:05] Daniel Kim: Yes, there is a cold start penalty. That's why we recommend either a small steady stream to secondaries or pre-warmed instances. For Dedicated customers we can provision warm pools in standby region under the SLA.
[03:20] Lena Ortiz: What's the SLA for Dedicated vs Hosted? We need numbers for procurement.
[03:27] Maya Patel: Hosted: we publish best-effort SLOs publicly — 99% uptime across regions historically, but standard commercial SLAs for enterprise customers come with Dedicated. Dedicated SLA can be 99.9% with credits for downtime, and multi-region redundancy options increase the SLA. Private is negotiated in the contract — often >99.95 when managed on-prem with proper infra.
[03:49] Mike Chen: Does SLA include tail latency guarantees (p95/p99)?
[03:52] Daniel Kim: We typically SLA availability and throughput; tail latency guarantees are harder because of customer workload variance. That said, for enterprise deals we add latency targets in the contract tied to a defined workload and offer remediation like capacity increases or model/quantization profiles.
[04:10] Sanjay Rao: So if we need hard p95 under 400ms, we need a runbook and maybe Dedicated with pre-warm?
[04:16] Daniel Kim: Exactly. We would run a benchmark with your prompt set, show the profile, then size Dedicated pools with reserved capacity and warm standby.
[04:24] Maya Patel: Also worth noting: routing can fallback to cheaper/compatible model variants — e.g., prod model -> quantized or distilled variant in a fallback event. That reduces cost and keeps availability, but may affect quality.
[04:38] Lena Ortiz: How transparent is that to the application? Can we see when a fallback happened?
[04:44] Daniel Kim: Yes, Console telemetry shows per-request model used, latency, and a reason code (health/fallback/overload). We also emit traces and audit logs for every routing decision.
[04:56] Mike Chen: Audit logs — are they immutable and retained how long? We need 1 year for our audit team.
[05:02] Maya Patel: Standard retention is 90 days for Hosted. For Dedicated/Private we can extend retention and ship logs to your S3 or SIEM; retention terms are part of the contract.
[05:14] Sanjay Rao: Let's talk about network failure modes. If a region has networking but compute is fine, do you have granular health checks (k8s pod vs instance vs infra) or it's coarse?
[05:26] Daniel Kim: Health checks operate at multiple levels — we check control-plane signals, model loading, and per-instance latency. The routing decision uses weighted signals so we can gradually shift traffic rather than a hard cutover.
[05:37] Lena Ortiz: Does Redwood support custom health check thresholds so we can tune sensitivity?
[05:41] Daniel Kim: Yes, for Dedicated and Private you can customize thresholds and automated rollback policies.
[05:48] Sanjay Rao: In the event of a partial outage — say one AZ degraded — do you do request retries automatically? What's the retry policy?
[05:58] Daniel Kim: We have built-in retries with exponential backoff for transient errors, and can fallback to model variants or other regions. Retry behavior is configurable per-route. For user-facing APIs we generally avoid aggressive retries to prevent amplification; we prefer fast failover to another healthy pool.
[06:15] Mike Chen: Can Redwood call our internal feature flagging service to gate routing? We want to keep control.
[06:20] Maya Patel: You can integrate routing decisions with your control plane via webhooks or use our API to programmatically set routing rules. Private deployments get deeper integrations.
[06:29] Sanjay Rao: For Private, if we host in our VPC, how is the control plane managed? Do you have a remote control plane that we can federate?
[06:36] Daniel Kim: We offer two Private modes: a customer-managed control plane that runs in your VPC with a lightweight agent, or an air-gapped on-prem package. The control plane speaks to Redwood for optional billing/updates but can be fully isolated if needed.
[06:50] Lena Ortiz: KMS and HSM — we need to manage keys.
[06:53] Maya Patel: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and can support HSM for encryption at rest. For Private, keys never leave your environment unless you opt-in.
[07:03] Sanjay Rao: Sounds good. A few more specifics: during a region failover, what happens to in-flight requests that were mid-token? Do you have retry-idempotency or resumable streams?
[07:13] Daniel Kim: For streaming generation, resumable streams are tricky. We support ephemeral session tokens and can resume from last committed KV state if the client persists the response offsets. Otherwise, streaming requests typically fail and you re-issue to the new region. We offer a best-effort approach to reduce duplicate tokens.
[07:34] Mike Chen: That's sort of expected — we might need to build a client-side handler.
[07:38] Maya Patel: We can share an SDK pattern for graceful handling of stream failover. That tends to be enough for most customers.
[07:45] Sanjay Rao: What about model version pinning during rollout — if you have automatic fallback to an older model, can we pin a route to a specific version?
[07:54] Daniel Kim: Yes. You can pin by model version. Rollouts support canary percentages and automatic rollback based on quality regressions or latency increases. We also support atomic rollouts across regions.
[08:06] Lena Ortiz: In case of a service degradation, do you provide a read-only degraded mode — e.g., only embeddings or only short responses to reduce tokens?
[08:14] Maya Patel: You can configure graceful degradation policies: token caps, shorter responses, or fallback to a smaller model. Policies are route-level and can be triggered by thresholds.
[08:23] Sanjay Rao: On the observability side — can we get per-token cost breakdown and traces tied to our internal IDs?
[08:30] Daniel Kim: Yes, per-token cost and latency breakdowns per-request are available. You can attach your correlation IDs, and traces flow through to the Console and exported logs.
[08:40] Mike Chen: For the benchmark, we'll provide a 5000-sample prompt set with expected latencies. Will Redwood simulate full load?
[08:47] Daniel Kim: We'll run both canonical perf tests and a replay of your prompt set to simulate warm/cold behavior. For Dedicated sizing we'll include peak concurrency and tail analyses.
[08:58] Lena Ortiz: Pricing — if we want a 3-month Dedicated pilot with multi-region standby, what's the rough ballpark?
[09:05] Maya Patel: Ballpark depends on model family and reserved GPU type. I'll follow up with a pricing sheet; typical pilots start with a modest commit that covers reserved capacity and warm standby. We'll include burst capacity and overage terms.
[09:18] Sanjay Rao: We have strict compliance needs — SOC2, ISO, and audit trail retention — you mentioned Hosted default is 90 days, can you extend?
[09:27] Maya Patel: Yes for Dedicated/Private we can extend retention and ship logs to your archive. We'll attach SOC2 and ISO artifacts in the follow-up.
[09:35] Mike Chen: One last thing — if the control plane itself loses contact with workers (e.g., network partition), do workers keep serving?
[09:44] Daniel Kim: Workers are designed to be resilient; they can serve in a degraded mode if control plane connectivity is lost, based on cached configs. For security-sensitive changes you might be blocked until control plane reconnects, but inference continues for already-loaded models.
[10:00] Sanjay Rao: Ok. I know we're only 10 minutes in but this has been helpful. Can we deep-dive on the failover sequence and health checks next?
[10:08] Maya Patel: Sure. Daniel, want to take the technical deep dive?
[10:12] Daniel Kim: Yep. I'll outline our detection and decision path: health signals, weighted routing, gradual shift, warm pools, and fallback policies.
[10:20] [TRANSITION TO TECHNICAL DEEP DIVE]
[10:30] Daniel Kim: On detection: we monitor per-instance latency and error rate, model load times, and infra-level metrics. We compute a composite health score and apply hysteresis so we don't flip-flop under flapping conditions.
[10:50] Lena Ortiz: Hysteresis meaning you have cooldown windows?
[10:53] Daniel Kim: Exactly. Configurable cooldown and recovery windows.
[11:00] Daniel Kim: For decisioning we rank candidate pools by health, cost, and region affinity; we prefer intra-region cheaper fallback before cross-region failover to avoid added network egress.
[11:16] Mike Chen: How granular is pool sizing? Can we have micro-shards to isolate noisy neighbors?
[11:21] Daniel Kim: Yes, Dedicated allows fine-grained pools per-route to prevent noisy neighbor impact. We also support container-level isolation and GPU pinning.
[11:31] Sanjay Rao: What about database / stateful dependencies during failover? Our inference pipeline calls a user-profile service that is in the same region.
[11:39] Daniel Kim: That's a common pattern. We recommend externalizing state to globally-available stores or using eventual-consistent fallbacks. During failover you'll need to ensure dependencies are reachable or design for degraded fallback (cached profiles).
[11:52] Lena Ortiz: Any real customer examples of region failovers? How long did it take and what mitigations worked?
[11:58] Maya Patel: We had a customer with a regional networking outage — warm standby in a secondary region cut over in ~18s for most traffic once health thresholds tripped, though some streaming requests needed re-issue. They used small steady traffic to keep caches warm which noticeably reduced cold latency during failover.
[12:18] Mike Chen: That 18s number is useful.
[12:20] Daniel Kim: Also for stateful sessions they externalized short-term session store to a global Redis, which reduced session loss.
[12:30] Sanjay Rao: Regarding fallback to model variants — can we control quality thresholds? I.e., only fallback if certain metrics are still within acceptable QA thresholds.
[12:39] Daniel Kim: Yes, you can set gating rules based on quality/regression tests; if fallback causes quality below the gate, we can block that fallback and instead route to alternate healthy pools.
[12:51] Lena Ortiz: For the QA gating, how do you evaluate quality in real-time?
[12:56] Daniel Kim: We have a lightweight eval runner that can execute sanity checks on sample prompt sets; for strict SLAs you can push a small canary and wait for evaluation results before broad rollout.
[13:10] Sanjay Rao: All right — procurement will want explicit failure-mode descriptions and runbooks. Can you provide a runbook template?
[13:16] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll send a runbook template and example playbooks.
[13:20] Mike Chen: For our benchmark, we want to test: normal load, failover to secondary region, fallback to quantized model, and full cold-start scenario. Is that doable in a single day?
[13:29] Daniel Kim: We can run a day-long engagement: morning baseline + afternoon failover and fallback tests. We'll need the prompt set and traffic profile ahead of time.
[13:38] Sanjay Rao: We'll send that today.
[13:40] Maya Patel: Great. A couple of quick notes: Hosted is fastest to get started, Dedicated buys you predictable capacity and SLAs, Private gives you full isolation and key control. For reliability/slo heavy workloads we often recommend starting Hosted for POC, then move to Dedicated pilot with warm standby if you need contractual SLAs.
[14:00] Lena Ortiz: Any gotchas around model quantization and fallbacks — e.g., hallucination frequency changes?
[14:07] Daniel Kim: Yes quantization/distillation can affect output. We recommend regression tests and quality monitoring tied to eval sets. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations on which quantized variants perform best for a workload.
[14:22] Mike Chen: How does Redwood handle throttling under high load — do you shed traffic or queue? We prefer graceful shedding with explicit 429s rather than large latencies.
[14:31] Daniel Kim: We prefer shedding with clear 429/503 semantics and provide backoff headers and retry windows. For Dedicated we can configure burst capacity and queue depth.
[14:41] Sanjay Rao: For a production incident, what's the communication cadence? Do you provide incident pages and postmortems?
[14:47] Maya Patel: Yes, for enterprise customers we provide incident notifications, status pages, and post-incident reports. For Dedicated we can include a joint postmortem with runbook steps and remediation actions.
[14:58] Lena Ortiz: One procurement question — if we require 1 year of audit logs and extended retention, any additional costs?
[15:05] Maya Patel: Usually yes — extended retention and storage egress have associated costs; we'll include that in the quote.
[15:12] Mike Chen: Any limitations on model size or sequence length in multi-region scenarios?
[15:17] Daniel Kim: Not inherently, but longer sequences increase KV sizes and cache warm-up time; longer contexts may exacerbate cold penalty during failover. We size Dedicated pools accordingly.
[15:30] Sanjay Rao: Let's recap next steps. We'll: send prompt set and traffic profile, want SOC2 docs, and run the benchmark.
[15:38] Maya Patel: Correct. Daniel will run the benchmark, I'll send the security pack and pilot pricing. We'll aim to reconvene after the benchmark and share the results.
[15:49] Sanjay Rao: Sounds good. Thank you both.
[15:52] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by end of week with docs.
[15:56] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]
